sports.football-analytics.expected-goals.title: The accountant who proved passing was pointless, wrongly
sports.football-analytics.expected-goals.hook: The first man to put football in a spreadsheet used it to argue against passing. His data said the opposite.
sports.football-analytics.expected-goals.author: author-sports-niche-1
sports.football-analytics.expected-goals.body:
Charles Reep (1904–2002) was an RAF wing commander who spent decades in English grandstands coding every pass by hand. In 1968 he and the statistician Bernard Benjamin published the result in the *Journal of the Royal Statistical Society*: the founding document of football analytics, with a textbook error for a conclusion.

Reep found that fewer than 80% of goals came from moves of three passes or fewer, and read it as proof that football should be played long and direct. Passing is waste.

Look at the denominator. In the same data, 91.5% of *all* moves were three passes or fewer. Short moves produced 80% of the goals while making up 91.5% of the chances — so the rare long moves converted at a *higher* rate, not a lower one. Reep counted where goals came from and forgot to ask how often each kind of move was attempted.

People acted on it. Reep advised Brentford in 1951, caught Stan Cullis's eye at Wolves, and his ideas still underpinned Egil Olsen's Norway in the 1990s. The correction — normalise by opportunities, then price each one — is what everything since has been about, xG included.

recall.question: Reep saw that most goals came from short passing moves. What did he forget to divide by?
recall.answer: The number of moves of each length. Almost all moves were short (91.5%), so short moves scoring 80% of the goals means they converted *worse* per attempt than the rare long moves. Counting outcomes without counting opportunities is a base-rate error.

sources.title: Skill and Chance in Association Football
sources.author: Charles Reep and Bernard Benjamin

sports.football-analytics.expected-goals.title: Nobody has ever scored 0.79 of a goal
sports.football-analytics.expected-goals.hook: Every penalty in Opta's model is worth exactly 0.79 goals. Not this penalty — penalties.
sports.football-analytics.expected-goals.author: author-sports-niche-1
sports.football-analytics.expected-goals.body:
Opta gives every penalty the same value: 0.79 expected goals, the historical conversion rate. Not because *this* penalty is 79% likely, but because penalties as a class go in about four times in five. That is the whole trick of expected goals, and also the whole limitation.

An xG model looks at a shot and mostly ignores who took it. It sees distance, angle, body part, whether it came from a cross or a through ball, how much of the goal was visible, where the keeper was standing — Opta's version uses more than twenty such variables — and returns the fraction of historically similar shots that ended in the net. Add those fractions across a match and you have a sentence: *given the chances you created, this is what an average finisher would have scored.*

That number separates the two things a scoreline welds together: how many chances you made, and whether they went in. But an average is a property of a crowd, and no single shot is a crowd.

Here is what "the fraction of similar shots" is, as a model.
sports.football-analytics.expected-goals.rigor:
An xG model is a binary classifier fitted to hundreds of thousands of historical shots. Let $x_i$ collect the features of shot $i$ and fit

$$\Pr(\text{goal}\mid x)=\sigma(\beta^{\top}x),\qquad \sigma(z)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-z}}$$

by maximum likelihood — logistic regression, or a gradient-boosted tree doing the same job with interactions. A team's match xG is $\sum_i p_i$ with $p_i=\sigma(\beta^{\top}x_i)$.

Now make "an average is a property of a crowd" precise. Goals scored is a sum of Bernoulli draws, a Poisson-binomial variable, so

$$\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\sum_i G_i\right)=\sum_i p_i(1-p_i).$$

Twelve shots averaging $p=0.125$ give $\text{xG}=1.5$ and a standard deviation of $1.15$ goals. A team that "underperformed its xG by one" in a match has told you nothing at all. Run the same arithmetic over a season — 500 shots, $\text{xG}\approx 60$ — and the standard deviation is about 7. Only then does finishing skill poke above the noise.

One quiet assumption: that the draws are independent. A rebound is a shot conditioned on the shot before it. And a deeper problem is waiting — almost every minute of a football match contains no shot at all.

recall.question: A striker's shots this season total 14 xG and he has scored 9. What is the most defensible reading?

options.text: He is a bad finisher
options.why: one season of shots is far too few to separate finishing skill from variance.

options.text: Probably bad luck, possibly bad finishing, and the sample can't yet tell you which
options.why: the standard deviation on 14 xG is roughly 3 goals.

options.text: The model is broken
options.why: xG is an average over similar shots, so individual deviations are expected, not evidence of a bug.

sports.football-analytics.passing-networ.title: Remember graphs? A football team is one, and it has a cut vertex.
sports.football-analytics.passing-networ.hook: Eleven vertices, a few hundred directed edges. A football team is a small weighted digraph that runs for ninety minutes.
sports.football-analytics.passing-networ.author: author-sports-niche-1

reviewed.notes: Brandes is O(|V||E|) only unweighted; added the weighted bound, since the card uses weights.

sports.football-analytics.passing-networ.body:
Vertices and edges, an adjacency matrix, centrality. You met all of it abstractly. Now put eleven players on the vertices and let $A_{ij}$ be the number of passes from $i$ to $j$ during a match. Everything you know transfers, and it all means something.

Out-degree is involvement. In-degree is how much your team looks for you. The matrix is *asymmetric* — a full-back who receives twenty passes from his centre-back and returns three is a different animal from one who returns twenty.

The interesting measure is betweenness: the fraction of shortest paths between other players that run through you. Duch, Waitzman and Amaral built a version of this in PLoS ONE in 2010 that measures flow towards the opponent's goal rather than between arbitrary players. López Peña and Touchette ran closeness, betweenness and PageRank over the 2010 World Cup sides in 2012.

High betweenness is the mathematical name for a pivot — and for a vulnerability. If deleting one vertex disconnects the graph, you have just found the man the opposition should mark.

Here is what that deletion does, precisely.
sports.football-analytics.passing-networ.rigor:
Let $G=(V,E,w)$ be the weighted digraph with $V$ the eleven players and $w_{ij}=A_{ij}$ the pass counts. Define edge *distance* as $d_{ij}=1/w_{ij}$, so that heavily used lanes are short — a passing move travels the cheap edges.

Betweenness of $v$ is

$$C_B(v)=\sum_{s\neq v\neq t}\frac{\sigma_{st}(v)}{\sigma_{st}},$$

where $\sigma_{st}$ counts shortest $s\to t$ paths and $\sigma_{st}(v)$ those through $v$. Brandes's algorithm computes it in $O(|V||E|)$ unweighted and $O(|V||E|+|V|^{2}\log|V|)$ with weights — for eleven vertices, instant either way.

Now the football question as a graph question: how much worse is the team without $v$? Compare the sum of pairwise shortest-path distances in $G$ and in $G-v$. A vertex whose removal blows that sum up is a *cut-vertex-like* bottleneck — exactly what a pressing scheme tries to manufacture by taking one passing option away.

And the strength-of-connection idea from the eigenvector ranking returns here in a different suit: PageRank on this same matrix asks not "who touches it most" but "who does the ball keep coming back to", and those are not the same player.

recall.question: In a passing network, why is edge distance usually set to $1/w_{ij}$ rather than $w_{ij}$?

options.text: Because shortest-path measures treat small weights as cheap, and a heavily used passing lane should be cheap to travel
options.why: inverting turns "lots of passes" into "short".

options.text: Because pass counts can be zero
options.why: zero-weight edges are simply absent; that is not why the inversion is used.

options.text: Because betweenness requires a symmetric matrix
options.why: it does not; the passing digraph is deliberately asymmetric.

sports.football-analytics.pitch-control..title: The best pass on the pitch is often the one nobody made
sports.football-analytics.pitch-control..hook: Draw the map of everywhere your team would win the ball if it landed there. Football turns into a weather chart.
sports.football-analytics.pitch-control..author: author-sports-niche-1
sports.football-analytics.pitch-control..body:
Event data records what happened. Tracking cameras record where all twenty-two players were while it happened, many times a second, which lets you ask a stranger question: *if the ball appeared at that patch of grass right now, whose would it be?*

Answer it for every patch and you get a map — Spearman's pitch control, presented at MIT Sloan in 2017 and extended in 2018. Two coloured territories, breathing and shifting as players run, with contested grey seams between them. A midfielder who never touches the ball spends ninety minutes redrawing that map.

Suddenly you can grade the pass a player *didn't* play. Take every point he could have reached, weight it by the chance his team would keep the ball there and by what that zone is worth, and the difference between the best available option and the one he chose is a number. Scouts have always said "he sees the pass"; this is the first tool that can disagree with them.

The map comes out of ordinary kinematics.
sports.football-analytics.pitch-control..rigor:
For every point $r$ and player $i$, compute the shortest time $T_i(r)$ to arrive there from the player's current position $x_i$ and velocity $v_i$, subject to a reaction delay and caps on acceleration and top speed. Let $T_b(r)$ be the time for the ball to travel there.

The crude version is a hard comparison: $r$ belongs to the team whose fastest player satisfies $\min_i T_i(r)<T_b(r)$. Note what this degenerates to — if every player stands still with the same top speed, $T_i(r)\propto\lVert r-x_i\rVert$ and the map is exactly the Voronoi diagram of the players. Pitch control *is* a Voronoi diagram that knows about momentum.

The usable version is probabilistic, because arrival times are uncertain. Smooth the comparison,

$$P_i(r)=\sigma\!\left(\frac{T_b(r)-T_i(r)}{s}\right),$$

with $\sigma$ the logistic function and $s$ a timing-uncertainty scale of a fraction of a second, then normalise across all players so the two teams' control at $r$ sums to one.

Combine with episode 2's zone values and you have the expected value of a pass to $r$: control times threat, integrated over the pitch.

Beautiful, and still incomplete. None of this knows why the players are standing where they are.

recall.question: If every player froze in place and they all ran equally fast, what would a pitch-control map become?

options.text: The Voronoi diagram of the players' positions
options.why: time-to-arrive is then proportional to distance, so each point goes to its nearest player.

options.text: A uniform 50–50 split
options.why: control depends on positions, which are not symmetric between the teams.

options.text: The convex hull of each team
options.why: hulls describe shape, not who reaches a point first.

options.text: An expected-goals surface
options.why: xG values shots, not territory.

sports.football-analytics.poisson-models.title: Two Poissons get football almost exactly right, and fail at 0–0
sports.football-analytics.poisson-models.hook: Model goals as two independent Poisson counts and you predict almost every scoreline correctly — except the ones that decide seasons.
sports.football-analytics.poisson-models.author: author-sports-niche-1

reviewed.notes: Corrected which scorelines independent Poissons misfit (0-0 and 1-1 are under-predicted, not 1-0/0-1); added the negative sign of rho; repaired broken KaTeX cases rows.

sports.football-analytics.poisson-models.body:
Goals are rare and scattered through ninety minutes, which is the situation Poisson was invented for. So the simplest serious model of a football match is two Poisson counts: one for the home side with rate $\lambda$, one for the away side with rate $\mu$, drawn independently. Give every club an attack parameter and a defence parameter, add one constant for playing at home, fit by maximum likelihood, and you can price every scoreline in the league.

It is almost embarrassingly good. Almost — because the *independence* is a lie exactly where it matters. Count real results and the low-scoring draws — 0–0 and 1–1 — show up more often than two independent Poissons say, while 1–0 and 0–1 show up less. Low-scoring matches are not two separate stories; a tight game makes both teams cagey.

Dixon and Coles fixed it in 1997 with the minimum possible violence: one extra parameter that nudges only those four scorelines, plus a rule that last month counts more than last year.
sports.football-analytics.poisson-models.rigor:
Home and away rates for the match between $i$ and $j$:

$$\lambda=\exp(\alpha_i+\beta_j+\gamma),\qquad \mu=\exp(\alpha_j+\beta_i),$$

with $\alpha$ attack, $\beta$ defence, $\gamma$ home advantage. The Dixon–Coles likelihood for a result $(x,y)$ is the independent-Poisson product multiplied by

$$\tau_{\lambda,\mu}(x,y)=\begin{cases}1-\lambda\mu\rho & x=y=0\\ 1+\lambda\rho & x=0,\,y=1\\ 1+\mu\rho & x=1,\,y=0\\ 1-\rho & x=y=1\\ 1 & \text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$$

Setting $\rho=0$ recovers plain independent Poissons, so $\rho$ is a single, testable departure from independence, and the correction vanishes above one goal each. Fitted on real leagues $\hat\rho$ comes out negative, around $-0.13$: probability moves into 0–0 and 1–1 and out of 1–0 and 0–1, which is the cagey-game story in one number.

Their second idea matters just as much: weight each past match by $\phi(t)=e^{-\xi t}$, $t$ being how long ago it was played, so that the likelihood is a *local* one. Team strength is not a constant to be estimated; it is a slowly moving target, and $\xi$ says how fast you think it moves.

Their own test was a betting strategy on 1995–96 odds, and it returned a profit — the strongest thing you can say about a model of anything.

recall.question: What does the Dixon–Coles parameter $\rho$ do?

options.text: It makes goals arrive non-uniformly through the match
options.why: the Poisson rate is already constant by assumption; $\rho$ does not touch timing.

options.text: It adjusts the four scorelines with at most one goal each
options.why: exactly where independent Poissons misfit the data, and setting it to zero recovers plain independent Poissons.

options.text: It down-weights older matches
options.why: that is the separate time-decay term $\phi(t)=e^{-\xi t}$.

options.text: It measures home advantage
options.why: that is $\gamma$, which sits inside the home rate.

sources.title: Modelling Association Football Scores and Inefficiencies in the Football Betting Market
sources.author: Mark J. Dixon and Stuart G. Coles

sources.title: Predicting football results with statistical modelling: Dixon-Coles and time-weighting

sports.football-analytics.possession-val.title: The pass that made the goal possible gets nothing
sports.football-analytics.possession-val.hook: Expected goals prices the 25 shots in a match and nothing else. So what is the pass that made the goal possible worth?
sports.football-analytics.possession-val.author: author-sports-niche-1

reviewed.notes: Hook's unsourced '1,500 actions a match' cut; kept Opta's verified 25 shots.

sports.football-analytics.possession-val.body:
Expected goals has a blind spot the size of a football match. It scores shots. It says nothing about the turn, the switch of play, the tackle that started the move — most of what players do, and most of what scouts argue about.

In 2018 Karun Singh published a fix on his blog. Chop the pitch into a 16-by-12 grid, 192 zones, and ask a single question of each zone: if my team has the ball *here*, what is the chance this possession ends in a goal? A player in that zone will either shoot (worth his shot's xG) or move the ball (worth whatever the destination zone is worth). So the value of a zone is defined in terms of the values of other zones. Circular — and that circularity is the engine, not the bug.

The Leuven group went further. Their VAEP framework prices *every* action, defensive ones included, by how much it shifts the probability of scoring and of conceding over the next few actions. A recovery in your own half gets a price tag.

The circular definition is what makes this work. Here it is written down.
sports.football-analytics.possession-val.rigor:
Let $V(z)$ be the expected threat of zone $z$. In zone $z$ a player shoots with probability $s(z)$ and scores with probability $g(z)$, or moves with probability $m(z)=1-s(z)$ to zone $z'$ with transition probability $T(z\to z')$. Then

$$V(z)=s(z)\,g(z)+m(z)\sum_{z'}T(z\to z')\,V(z').$$

Singh solves it by setting $V\equiv 0$ and iterating; it converges in four or five passes. In matrix form $V=b+MTV$, so $V=(I-MT)^{-1}b$ — a linear solve whose inverse exists because possessions end: the chain is absorbing, $\|MT\|<1$.

The value of a pass is then just $V(\text{end})-V(\text{start})$, and you can hand a player his season total in goals-worth-of-progression.

VAEP (Decroos et al., KDD 2019) drops the grid and learns $\Pr(\text{score within }k\text{ actions})$ and $\Pr(\text{concede within }k)$ directly from the game state, then values an action as the change in the difference. Same idea, richer state, no zones.

And still a fiction: the model knows where the ball is, not where the other twenty-one players are standing.

recall.question: Why is expected threat defined circularly — the value of a zone in terms of the values of other zones — and why doesn't that break?
recall.answer: Because value flows backwards from goals: a zone is worth what you can reach from it. It doesn't break because possessions end, so the chain is absorbing and the fixed-point equation $V=b+MTV$ has a unique solution you can reach by iterating from zero.

sources.title: Actions Speak Louder than Goals: Valuing Player Actions in Soccer
sources.author: Decroos, Bransen, Van Haaren, Davis

sports.football-analytics.possession-val.title: Remember absorbing Markov chains? A football possession is one.
sports.football-analytics.possession-val.hook: An absorbing chain asks: starting here, where do I end up? Football asks: starting here, do I score?
sports.football-analytics.possession-val.author: author-sports-niche-1

reviewed.notes: Repaired a broken KaTeX block matrix (missing row break).

sports.football-analytics.possession-val.body:
When you met absorbing chains, the payoff question was: from this transient state, what is the probability I am eventually swallowed by *that* absorbing state? You solved it with the fundamental matrix and it felt like bookkeeping.

Now hand the chain a football. The transient states are the zones of the pitch — Karun Singh's expected-threat model uses a 16-by-12 grid, so 192 of them. There are exactly two absorbing states: **goal** and **possession lost**. A move is a transition between zones; a shot is a coin flip into one absorber or the other; a turnover is the other absorber.

The "value" of a zone that episode two defined circularly is not a new idea at all. It is the absorption probability of the goal state, starting from that zone. And the iteration Singh runs until it converges is just repeated multiplication by the transition matrix — the same computation you already did on a rat in a maze, run on a pitch instead.

The bookkeeping is the same bookkeeping.
sports.football-analytics.possession-val.rigor:
Order the states as transient $Z$ (the 192 zones) then absorbing $\{\text{goal},\text{lost}\}$, giving

$$P=\begin{pmatrix}Q & R\\ 0 & I\end{pmatrix}.$$

If $\rho(Q)<1$ — true here because every possession ends — the fundamental matrix $N=(I-Q)^{-1}=\sum_{k\ge0}Q^{k}$ exists, $N_{ij}$ counts expected visits to zone $j$ before absorption starting from $i$, and the absorption probabilities are $B=NR$. Expected threat is the goal column of $B$:

$$V=(I-Q)^{-1}r_{\text{goal}},$$

which is exactly the fixed point $V=r_{\text{goal}}+QV$ that Singh reaches by starting at $V\equiv 0$ and iterating. Power iteration on an absorbing chain, four or five sweeps, done.

One honest caveat the chain forces into the open: Markov means the value of a zone depends on the zone alone, not on how the ball arrived. Real football is emphatically not memoryless — that is precisely why the later models threw the grid away and learned from the full game state.

recall.question: In the Markov picture of a possession, what are the absorbing states, and what quantity is "expected threat"?
recall.answer: The absorbing states are *goal* and *possession lost*. Expected threat for a zone is the probability of being absorbed into *goal* starting from that zone — the goal column of $B=(I-Q)^{-1}R$.

sports.football-analytics.pressing-tacti.title: A number that goes down when you press harder
sports.football-analytics.pressing-tacti.hook: PPDA measures a press with a ratio anyone can compute. That is exactly why it gets misread.
sports.football-analytics.pressing-tacti.author: author-sports-niche-1

reviewed.notes: PPDA dated to Colin Trainor's StatsBomb article of July 2014, not 'around 2013'.

sports.football-analytics.pressing-tacti.body:
Pressing is the hardest thing in football to count, because a successful press produces *nothing*: no tackle, no interception, no event at all. The opponent simply declines to play the pass.

The workaround, Colin Trainor's on StatsBomb in July 2014, is PPDA — passes allowed per defensive action. Count the opponent's passes in the attacking sixty per cent of the pitch, divide by your tackles, interceptions, fouls and challenges there. Let them pass eight times per intervention and you are hounding them; fourteen and you are sitting off. Note the direction: a *lower* PPDA means a *more* aggressive press. Half the bad analysis in football comes from that inverted sign.

And the metric has a hole in the middle of it. A team so intimidating that the opponent never plays forward at all records almost no defensive actions and almost no opponent passes, and PPDA shrugs.

Every number in this series has the same shape of flaw. Here is the ledger.
sports.football-analytics.pressing-tacti.rigor:
$$\mathrm{PPDA}=\frac{\#\{\text{opponent passes in the attacking } 60\%\}}{\#\{\text{tackles}+\text{interceptions}+\text{challenges}+\text{fouls there}\}}$$

The denominator is the problem: it counts *attempts to intervene*, which is a proxy for pressure and not pressure itself. Deterrence is invisible to it, and so is a press that works by shaping passes rather than stopping them.

Run the same audit back through the series. Episode 1: xG is an average over a crowd of similar shots, so per-match deviations are mostly variance, and the model does not know that this striker is Haaland. Episode 2: expected threat and VAEP price actions using only ball-state, so an identical pass into an identical zone scores identically whether it broke a line or not. Episode 3: pitch control knows where the players are, never why — a defender holding a deliberate trap looks exactly like a defender out of position.

The honest summary is that these models measure *how much a situation is worth on average*, and football is played one situation at a time. That is not a reason to ignore them. It is the reason nobody has ever scored 0.79 of a goal, and the reason you still want to know which shots are worth 0.79.

recall.question: A side switches to an aggressive high press. What should happen to its PPDA?

options.text: It should fall
options.why: PPDA counts opponent passes per defensive action, so more intervention per pass makes the ratio smaller.

options.text: It should rise
options.why: that is the common misreading; the metric is a ratio of passes allowed, not of pressure applied.

options.text: It should stay flat
options.why: pressing changes both parts of the ratio, but not by the same factor.

sources.title: Defensive Metrics: Measuring the Intensity of a High Press

sports.football-analytics.ratings-elo.fi.title: The ranking you could climb by not playing
sports.football-analytics.ratings-elo.fi.hook: Romania hired a ranking consultant and then refused to play football. It worked.
sports.football-analytics.ratings-elo.fi.author: author-sports-niche-1
sports.football-analytics.ratings-elo.fi.body:
Between 2006 and 2018, FIFA ranked national teams on an average of points earned over four years. Average. Which means a win could cost you points — beat a weak side by less than your average, and your average falls.

Teams noticed. In the 2010s the ranking was openly gamed by *refusing fixtures*: since World Cup seeding depended on the December ranking, the optimal strategy before a draw was to play as little as possible, especially against weaker opponents. Romania went as far as appointing a ranking consultant and playing a single friendly in the year before a draw.

A metric that punishes participation is a metric nobody should have shipped. On 16 August 2018, after the World Cup in Russia, FIFA replaced it with an Elo system — the one Arpad Elo built for American chess in 1960 and FIDE adopted in 1970.

Elo has a property the old system lacked: it is a transfer. Points you win are points your opponent loses, so beating anyone is weakly positive and playing more games is never itself a penalty. The incentive to hide disappears because the arithmetic no longer rewards it.

recall.question: Why could a national team's FIFA ranking fall after winning a match under the pre-2018 system?

options.text: Ratings were an average of points per match, so a win worth less than your current average pulls the average down
options.why: a classic Goodhart failure.

options.text: Friendlies did not count at all
options.why: they counted, just at a low weight; the problem was averaging, not exclusion.

options.text: Only goal difference mattered
options.why: goals scored were dropped from the formula in 2006.

sports.football-analytics.ratings-elo.re.title: Remember Bayes? Every Elo rating is a posterior that forgot its error bars.
sports.football-analytics.ratings-elo.re.hook: New rating = old rating + K × (what happened − what you expected). That is Bayes with the variance nailed shut.
sports.football-analytics.ratings-elo.re.author: author-sports-niche-1

reviewed.notes: Elo's own model used a normal curve; the logistic form came later. Corrected.

sports.football-analytics.ratings-elo.re.body:
Bayes told you how to change your mind: start with a belief, see evidence, move in proportion to how surprising the evidence was. Elo ratings do exactly that, in one line, and have done since 1960.

A rating is a belief about strength. Before a match, the ratings imply an expected score $E$ — Elo's own model used a normal curve; the logistic version everyone now uses is calibrated so that 400 points of gap means ten-to-one odds. After the match you observed $S$: 1, 0.5 or 0. The update is

$$R' = R + K\,(S-E).$$

Old belief, plus a step proportional to the surprise. If the result was exactly what you expected, $S=E$ and nothing moves — a Bayesian update with zero information content.

What Elo throws away is the *uncertainty*. A real posterior narrows as evidence accumulates; Elo's $K$ is a constant, so a player with 800 games and a player with 8 move by the same amount. Mark Glickman's Glicko system restores it by tracking a rating deviation alongside the rating, which is the Kalman-filter version of the same idea.

And there is a second reading of that one line.
sports.football-analytics.ratings-elo.re.rigor:
Write $p=\Pr(A\text{ wins})=\sigma\!\left(\frac{\ln 10}{400}(R_A-R_B)\right)$, which is Elo's $E_A=\left(1+10^{(R_B-R_A)/400}\right)^{-1}$ in logistic form.

Treat the result $S\in\{0,1\}$ as Bernoulli and take the log-likelihood $\ell=S\ln p+(1-S)\ln(1-p)$. Differentiating a logistic log-likelihood with respect to its linear predictor gives the residual, so

$$\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial R_A}=\frac{\ln 10}{400}\,(S-p).$$

A gradient-ascent step of size $\eta$ is therefore $\Delta R_A=\eta\frac{\ln 10}{400}(S-E)$ — which is Elo's rule with $K=\eta\ln 10/400$.

So the same three symbols are three things at once: a Bayesian update with fixed gain, one step of stochastic gradient ascent on a Bradley–Terry logistic model, and a bookkeeping rule a physics professor designed for chess clubs to run by hand. $K$ is simultaneously the prior's stubbornness and the learning rate, which is why every league argues about it: small $K$ trusts history, large $K$ trusts last Sunday.

recall.question: In $R'=R+K(S-E)$, what is $K$ doing?

options.text: Converting between points and goals
options.why: Elo's inputs are results, not margins; $K$ has nothing to do with goals.

options.text: Setting how much one result moves your belief
options.why: it is simultaneously the fixed gain of a Bayesian update and the learning rate of a gradient step, which is why it is a tuning choice, not a fact.

options.text: Normalising the ratings so they sum to a constant
options.why: ratings are already a zero-sum transfer; $K$ scales the transfer, it does not enforce it.

sports.history.latam-football.el-94.title: El 5-0, y después
sports.history.latam-football.el-94.hook: En 1993 Colombia le ganó 5-0 a Argentina en Buenos Aires y Pelé la puso como favorita del Mundial. Nueve meses después todo se había ido.
sports.history.latam-football.el-94.author: author-sports-niche-1

reviewed.notes: Vague 'amenazas' replaced by the documented Gabriel Jaime Gomez threats; sentence reduction specified (43 to 23 anos); added Argentina's 33-match home record.

sports.history.latam-football.el-94.body:
5 de septiembre de 1993, Estadio Monumental. Rincón dos, Asprilla dos, Valencia uno: Colombia 5, Argentina 0 — la primera derrota de Argentina como local en 33 partidos de eliminatorias. Pelé señaló a Colombia como favorita para ganar el Mundial de Estados Unidos.

Lo que siguió fue lo contrario de una historia deportiva. En el Mundial, el volante Gabriel Jaime Gómez recibió amenazas telefónicas contra su familia y Maturana lo sacó del once. El 22 de junio de 1994, contra Estados Unidos, un centro raso se le metió a Andrés Escobar en su propio arco al minuto 34. Stewart hizo el segundo, Valencia descontó a los 90, y Colombia quedó eliminada.

El 2 de julio, en Medellín, Andrés Escobar fue asesinado. Humberto Muñoz Castro fue condenado a 43 años, rebajados después a 23. Lo documentado judicialmente es una discusión a la salida de un bar, con el autogol de por medio; la versión de que detrás hubo mafias de apuestas circula desde entonces y nunca se probó.

Al volver de Estados Unidos, Escobar había dicho que la vida no termina ahí, que era apenas un partido de fútbol. Tenía 27 años.

recall.question: ¿Qué está judicialmente documentado sobre el asesinato de Andrés Escobar y qué no?
recall.answer: Documentado: fue asesinado el 2 de julio de 1994 en Medellín, tras una discusión a la salida de un bar en la que se le reprochó el autogol; Humberto Muñoz Castro fue condenado a 43 años, rebajados después a 23, y salió libre en 2005. No probado: la hipótesis de que el crimen respondiera a apuestas perdidas, que circula desde entonces sin haberse acreditado ante un tribunal.

sports.history.latam-football.el-dorado.title: Cinco años en los que Bogotá fue la capital del fútbol mundial
sports.history.latam-football.el-dorado.hook: Entre 1949 y 1954 el mejor fútbol del mundo se jugó en Bogotá, y fue porque Colombia estaba expulsada de la FIFA.
sports.history.latam-football.el-dorado.author: author-sports-niche-1
sports.history.latam-football.el-dorado.body:
La Dimayor se fundó el 26 de junio de 1948 y la FIFA respondió expulsando a Colombia. Esa expulsión, que debía ser un castigo, fue el negocio del siglo: fuera de la FIFA, los clubes colombianos no estaban obligados a pagarle un peso a nadie por fichar a un jugador. Podían simplemente ofrecerle sueldo.

Y al mismo tiempo, en Argentina, los futbolistas agremiados estaban en huelga contra el gobierno de Perón. Un mercado entero de cracks sin trabajo, y un país que podía contratarlos sin indemnizaciones.

Llegó primero Adolfo Pedernera, ídolo de la selección argentina; luego trajo a Néstor Rossi y a un delantero joven llamado Alfredo Di Stéfano. Ese Millonarios fue el Ballet Azul, y jugó amistosos contra Real Madrid y Vasco da Gama ante estadios llenos. Di Stéfano salió de Bogotá directo a ganar cinco Copas de Europa.

La fiesta terminó en una mesa de negociación: el Pacto de Lima de 1951 devolvió a Colombia al redil con la condición de que los extranjeros regresaran a sus ligas en 1954. Los clubes colombianos no pagaron nada. Habían alquilado a los mejores del mundo durante cinco años.

recall.question: ¿Por qué la expulsión de la FIFA fue una ventaja para el fútbol colombiano entre 1949 y 1954?
recall.answer: Porque fuera de la FIFA los clubes de la Dimayor no estaban obligados a pagar derechos de transferencia: podían contratar a cualquier jugador ofreciéndole solamente un salario. Coincidió con la huelga de los futbolistas argentinos, que dejó libres a decenas de estrellas.

sports.history.latam-football.el-maracan.title: El 16 de julio de 1950 no hubo final
sports.history.latam-football.el-maracan.hook: Brasil solo necesitaba empatar. Uruguay ganó 2-1 y ciento setenta mil personas salieron del estadio en silencio.
sports.history.latam-football.el-maracan.author: author-sports-niche-1

reviewed.notes: Varela's line found verbatim in the source, so it is now a real quotation.

sports.history.latam-football.el-maracan.body:
Detalle que casi nadie sabe: el Mundial de 1950 no terminó con una final. Terminó con un cuadrangular, y el último partido quedó decisivo por casualidad aritmética. Brasil llegaba primero y le bastaba el empate. Uruguay tenía que ganar.

El Maracanã, estrenado para ese torneo, registró 173.850 entradas pagas; algunas fuentes hablan de casi doscientas mil personas adentro. Los diarios de Río ya habían impreso portadas con Brasil campeón.

Friaça marcó a los 47 minutos. Y ahí ocurre la escena que los uruguayos cuentan como fundacional: Obdulio Varela, el capitán, tomó la pelota y se fue a discutirle el gol al árbitro —que era correcto— solamente para enfriar el estadio. Cuando el juego se reanudó, el ruido se había apagado. Schiaffino empató a los 66. Ghiggia, a los 79, metió el segundo entre el poste y el guardameta Barbosa.

Ciento setenta mil personas se quedaron mudas. Años después Varela lo resumió sin épica: «si ese partido lo jugábamos otras 99 veces, las perdíamos todas, pero ese día nos tocó el partido 100».

recall.question: ¿Por qué a Brasil le bastaba con empatar el 16 de julio de 1950?
recall.answer: Porque el Mundial de 1950 se definió por un cuadrangular final, no por una final eliminatoria. Brasil encabezaba la tabla y sumaba con el empate; Uruguay estaba obligado a ganar.

sources.title: Uruguay v Brazil (1950 FIFA World Cup)

sports.history.latam-football.la-mano-y-.title: Cuatro minutos, dos goles, un problema moral
sports.history.latam-football.la-mano-y-.hook: Cuatro minutos separan el gol más tramposo del Mundial del mejor gol de la historia. Los hizo el mismo hombre.
sports.history.latam-football.la-mano-y-.author: author-sports-niche-1
sports.history.latam-football.la-mano-y-.body:
22 de junio de 1986, Estadio Azteca, cuartos de final. Argentina e Inglaterra jugaban cuatro años después de Malvinas y todo el mundo lo sabía.

Minuto 51: Maradona salta con Shilton y mete la pelota con el puño izquierdo. El árbitro no lo ve. En la rueda de prensa posterior, Maradona lo describió con una frase que se volvió idioma: fue *«un poco con la cabeza de Maradona y otro poco con la mano de Dios»*.

Minuto 55: recibe de espaldas en su propio campo, gira entre dos, y atraviesa media cancha driblando ingleses hasta dejar sentado a Shilton. Las crónicas no se ponen de acuerdo sobre cuántos rivales eludió —cinco, seis— pero sí sobre lo demás. En 2002 una votación de FIFA con 341.460 participantes lo eligió Gol del Siglo.

La banda sonora es de Víctor Hugo Morales: *«Barrilete cósmico… ¿de qué planeta viniste para dejar en el camino a tanto inglés…?»*.

Lo raro no es que un hombre pueda hacer las dos cosas. Es que las hizo en el mismo partido, con cuatro minutos de diferencia, y que nadie ha conseguido elegir cuál lo define.

recall.question: ¿Qué dijo Maradona en la rueda de prensa sobre el primer gol?
recall.answer: Que había sido «un poco con la cabeza de Maradona y otro poco con la mano de Dios» — una confesión disfrazada de chiste, que terminó bautizando la jugada.

sources.title: Argentina v England (1986 FIFA World Cup)

sports.history.tactical-evolution.the-of.title: Three became two, and the centre-back was born
sports.history.tactical-evolution.the-of.hook: One word changed in the offside law in 1925. English football scored 1,673 more goals the next season.
sports.history.tactical-evolution.the-of.author: author-sports-niche-1

reviewed.notes: Cut the unsourced 'offside forty times a match'; WM dominance corrected to standard from the late 1930s and lasting a generation.

sports.history.tactical-evolution.the-of.body:
Before 1925 an attacker needed three opponents between him and the goal line. Defences had turned this into a weapon: two full-backs stepping up in unison, killing move after move before it started. It was legal, effective and unwatchable.

The law was changed from three to two. The effect was immediate and enormous. English league clubs scored 4,700 goals in 1,848 matches in 1924–25; the following season, over the same number of matches, they scored 6,373.

Defences had to reorganise or drown, and Herbert Chapman's Arsenal reorganised hardest. The centre-half, until then a roaming playmaker in the 2-3-5 pyramid, was pulled back between the full-backs to sit as a third defender: the "stopper". Two inside-forwards dropped to link play. Written out, the shape makes a W and an M. By the late 1930s most English clubs had adopted the WM, and it stayed the default for a generation.

The modern centre-back — the defender whose only job is defending — is not a football idea. It is an artefact of a rule change made to stop a loophole.

recall.question: What did the 1925 offside change actually do to the game?

options.text: It cut the required defenders from three to two
options.why: goals jumped by about a third, and defences answered by dropping the centre-half back as a dedicated stopper.

options.text: It introduced the offside line at the halfway mark
options.why: that restriction came much earlier and is a separate rule.

options.text: It made offside apply only in the penalty area
options.why: offside has never been confined to the box.

sports.history.world-cup.pickles.title: The World Cup was found by a dog called Pickles
sports.history.world-cup.pickles.hook: Scotland Yard could not find the World Cup. A dog sniffing a hedge in South London found it in seven days.
sports.history.world-cup.pickles.author: author-sports-niche-1

reviewed.notes: Dropped the unsourceable comparison with England's winning bonus; replaced with Corbett's and Pickles's documented rewards.

sports.history.world-cup.pickles.body:
On 20 March 1966, four months before England hosted the World Cup, the Jules Rimet Trophy was stolen from a stamp exhibition at Westminster Central Hall. Scotland Yard had nothing.

On 27 March a black-and-white collie called Pickles stopped at a hedge in Beulah Hill, South London, and would not move. Under it, wrapped in newspaper, was the trophy. His owner collected nearly £5,000 — enough to buy a house. Pickles got a year of free dog food, a film role, and an invitation to England's victory banquet.

recall.question: How was the stolen Jules Rimet Trophy recovered in 1966?
recall.answer: By accident. A collie called Pickles found it wrapped in newspaper under a hedge in Beulah Hill, South London, on 27 March 1966, a week after it was stolen from a stamp exhibition. His owner's reward bought a house; Pickles got a year of free dog food and a seat at the victory banquet.

sports.stats.betting-markets.remember-ef.title: Remember efficient markets? Football odds are the cleanest test ever built.
sports.stats.betting-markets.remember-ef.hook: A bookmaker's odds are a probability forecast with money behind it — and they add up to more than one on purpose.
sports.stats.betting-markets.remember-ef.author: author-sports-niche-1
sports.stats.betting-markets.remember-ef.body:
Efficient markets are hard to test on stocks, because nobody knows what a stock is "really" worth. Betting markets do not have that problem. Every contract expires at full time, and the truth is printed on the scoreboard. If prices aggregate information, this is where it should show.

Mostly, they do. Bookmakers' implied probabilities track outcomes closely enough that beating them consistently is very hard, and public models that look brilliant on paper usually lose money once you subtract the spread.

Two structural facts spoil the purity. First, the prices are not probabilities: invert the odds on every outcome and they sum to more than one. The excess is the *overround*, the bookmaker's margin, and it is the reason a merely-as-good-as-the-market forecast loses steadily. Second, there is a real, decades-old anomaly — the favourite–longshot bias, in which long shots are systematically overbet and favourites underbet. Snowberg and Wolfers argued in 2010 that it looks less like risk-loving preferences and more like people misperceiving small probabilities.

The arithmetic of that margin decides whether any edge is usable.
sports.stats.betting-markets.remember-ef.rigor:
For decimal odds $o_i$ on mutually exclusive outcomes, the implied (unnormalised) probabilities are $1/o_i$ and

$$\text{overround}=\sum_i \frac{1}{o_i}-1 .$$

A three-way football market quoted at $2.10 / 3.40 / 3.80$ gives $0.476+0.294+0.263=1.033$: a 3.3% margin. Normalising, $\hat{p}_i=(1/o_i)/\sum_j(1/o_j)$, recovers the bookmaker's implied probabilities.

Your expected return staking on outcome $i$ at true probability $p_i$ is $p_i o_i-1$. Break-even needs $p_i>1/o_i$, so you must beat the *quoted* probability, which already exceeds the bookmaker's own belief by the margin. With a 3% overround spread over three outcomes, a forecast one percentage point better than the market on a near-even chance still loses.

That is the sharp form of the efficiency claim here: not "the market is right", but "the market is right to within the spread", which is all that efficiency ever meant and exactly what makes it so exhausting to exploit.

recall.question: Odds of 2.10, 3.40 and 3.80 are offered on the three results of a match. Do the implied probabilities sum to one, and what is the difference called?
recall.answer: No — $1/2.10+1/3.40+1/3.80\approx 1.033$. The 3.3% excess is the overround, the bookmaker's margin. It is why a forecast that merely matches the market's accuracy still loses money.

sources.title: Explaining the Favorite-Longshot Bias: Is it Risk-Love or Misperceptions?
sources.author: Erik Snowberg and Justin Wolfers

sports.stats.home-advantage.empty-stadiu.title: The referees changed, and nobody had told them anything
sports.stats.home-advantage.empty-stadiu.hook: A tragedy in Catania emptied Italian stadiums in 2007 — and handed economists the cleanest test of crowd pressure ever run.
sports.stats.home-advantage.empty-stadiu.author: author-sports-niche-1
sports.stats.home-advantage.empty-stadiu.body:
On 2 February 2007 a police officer, Filippo Raciti, was killed during rioting at the Sicilian derby between Catania and Palermo. Italian football stopped. When it restarted, clubs whose grounds did not meet safety standards were ordered to play their home matches behind closed doors.

Two Swedish economists, Per Pettersson-Lidbom and Mikael Priks, saw what nobody else did: a natural experiment. Same league, same teams, same squads, same referees — and, for a handful of fixtures, no crowd. Everything that usually gets blamed for home advantage (travel, pitch familiarity, the players' nerves) was held fixed. Only the spectators vanished.

The refereeing changed. With the stands empty, the tilt in fouls and cards toward the home side shrank sharply. Their 2010 paper in *Economics Letters* puts it plainly: referees "exhibited home bias caused by social pressure when spectators were present."

Which reframes home advantage entirely. Part of it was never about the home team at all. It was about twenty thousand people leaning on one person in the middle who was trying very hard to be fair.

recall.question: What made the empty Italian stadiums of 2007 a *natural experiment* rather than just an anecdote?
recall.answer: The closures were imposed for reasons unrelated to any team's quality or form — stadium safety compliance — so the presence of a crowd was as good as randomly assigned across matches. Everything else about home advantage stayed fixed, leaving crowd pressure as the only thing that moved.

sources.title: Behavior under social pressure: Empty Italian stadiums and referee bias
sources.author: Per Pettersson-Lidbom and Mikael Priks

sports.stats.home-advantage.the-pandemic.title: The best experiment in sports science was an accident
sports.stats.home-advantage.the-pandemic.hook: In 2020 football played 83 Bundesliga matches with nobody watching. Home advantage went negative.
sports.stats.home-advantage.the-pandemic.author: author-sports-niche-1
sports.stats.home-advantage.the-pandemic.body:
The Sicilian closures of 2007 gave economists a few dozen silent matches. In 2020 a pandemic gave them entire leagues.

Tilp and Thaller took the 2019/20 Bundesliga, split it at the shutdown, and measured home advantage as the share of all points that went to home teams. With crowds, across 223 matches: 54.35%. In the 83 "ghost games" after the restart: 44.1%. Home teams went from taking more than half the points on offer to taking less than half. The advantage did not shrink. It inverted.

The referees' side of the ledger is sharper still. With spectators, home sides collected 44.85% of yellow cards and away sides 55.15% — a visible tilt. Without spectators: 51.1% and 48.9%, statistically indistinguishable from even.

One league, one season, small samples, and other things changed too (no travel fatigue for anyone, matches rescheduled, substitutions expanded). But the direction replicates across leagues, and it lines up with the Italian result.

The arithmetic of what "44.1%" is measuring is worth doing slowly.
sports.stats.home-advantage.the-pandemic.rigor:
Home advantage here is $\text{HA}=P_{\text{home}}/(P_{\text{home}}+P_{\text{away}})$, the fraction of all league points taken by home sides. Under perfect symmetry $\text{HA}=0.5$; the 2018/19 benchmark was 57.63%.

Two cautions an econometrician should raise. First, this is a before/after comparison within one season, not a randomised assignment: the shutdown coincides with a fixture pile-up, a long layoff and five-substitution rules, all of which plausibly move outcomes. The Italian 2007 design is cleaner precisely because closed-door and open matches ran *in parallel*.

Second, sample size. With 83 matches and roughly $3\times 83$ points at stake, the standard error on a proportion near $0.5$ is about $\sqrt{0.25/249}\approx 0.032$ — three percentage points. A 10-point swing clears that, but only just, and a single league-season is one draw from the distribution, not the distribution.

The right reading: crowds move referees, robustly; how much of *home advantage* that explains is still being argued.

recall.question: Why is the Italian 2007 closed-door study a cleaner design than the 2020 Bundesliga comparison?

options.text: Closed-door and normal matches ran during the same period, so season-wide changes cannot explain the difference
options.why: the 2020 split coincides with a layoff, new substitution rules and a congested calendar.

options.text: It used more matches
options.why: it used far fewer; the strength is in the comparison group, not the sample size.

options.text: It measured cards rather than points
options.why: both studies looked at cards; the metric is not what separates the designs.

sources.title: Covid-19 Has Turned Home Advantage Into Home Disadvantage in the German Soccer Bundesliga
sources.author: Markus Tilp and Sigrid Thaller

sports.stats.hot-hand.four-coin-flips.title: Four flips, and the coin appears to hate streaks
sports.stats.hot-hand.four-coin-flips.hook: A fair coin, four flips, one innocent-looking question. The answer is not one half, and it took 33 years to notice.
sports.stats.hot-hand.four-coin-flips.author: author-sports-niche-1
sports.stats.hot-hand.four-coin-flips.body:
Take a fair coin and flip it four times. Write the sequence down — say **H T H H**.

Now do what every hot-hand study does. Find every flip that came *immediately after a head*, and ask what fraction of those flips are themselves heads. In **H T H H** the flips following a head are the second (T) and the fourth (H), so the fraction is one half.

Do this for all sixteen possible sequences, throwing away the ones where no flip ever follows a head. Average the fraction across the sequences that remain.

The coin has no memory. Each flip is 50-50 and independent of everything before it. So the average of that fraction must be 0.5.

Make your guess before you look. What is it actually?

recall.question: What is the average fraction, and what is wrong with the reasoning above?
recall.answer: It is $17/42\approx 0.405$, not $0.5$. The three-flip version of the same puzzle gives exactly $5/12$. Nothing is wrong with the coin: the *procedure* is biased. Asking "what followed a head?" in a short finite sequence selects flips in a way that systematically under-counts heads, because a head you have already used up cannot be reused. Miller and Sanjurjo proved this in Econometrica in 2018 — and it is the same statistic that was used to declare the hot hand an illusion.

sources.title: Surprised by the Hot Hand Fallacy? A Truth in the Law of Small Numbers
sources.author: Joshua B. Miller and Adam Sanjurjo

sports.stats.hot-hand.the-fallacy-had-a-.title: The hot hand fallacy had a fallacy in it
sports.stats.hot-hand.the-fallacy-had-a-.hook: For 33 years the hot hand was the textbook example of humans seeing patterns in noise. Then someone checked the estimator.
sports.stats.hot-hand.the-fallacy-had-a-.author: author-sports-niche-1

reviewed.notes: Bias holds for n>=3, not every finite n (n=2 is unbiased); the 100-shot claim restated as the ~8pp gap in GVT's three-in-a-row comparison.

sports.stats.hot-hand.the-fallacy-had-a-.body:
In 1985 Gilovich, Vallone and Tversky took Philadelphia 76ers shooting records and a controlled shooting experiment at Cornell, looked at what happened after a make, found no lift, and concluded that the hot hand is something fans invent. It became the canonical demonstration that human pattern-detection is broken — cited in every behavioural economics course, Tversky's own favourite result.

The measure they used was: among shots taken right after a made shot, what fraction went in? Compare it to the overall rate. Sensible. Obviously unbiased.

It is not unbiased. In a *finite* sequence, selecting the shots that follow a make is not a neutral act of looking; it is a filter that pulls the expected hit rate below the true rate. Joshua Miller and Adam Sanjurjo proved it and published in Econometrica in 2018. Correct for the bias and the Cornell data flips sign: a hot-hand effect of roughly 13 percentage points, with a wide confidence interval.

The bias is small, exact, and easy to state.

recall.question: Why is "the hit rate on shots following a make" a biased estimator of the true hit rate?

options.text: Because makes and misses are not independent in real basketball
options.why: that is the hypothesis being tested, so it cannot be the source of the bias; the bias appears even for a fair coin.

options.text: Because in a finite sequence, conditioning on "follows a make" samples without replacement and systematically under-counts makes
options.why: the bias is a property of the selection rule, not of the shooter.

options.text: Because players take harder shots after a make
options.why: a real effect, but it does not explain why a simulated coin shows the same shortfall.

sports.stats.moneyball.the-part-that-was.title: The 2002 Oakland A's were not smarter. They were shopping in the right aisle.
sports.stats.moneyball.the-part-that-was.hook: Moneyball's real claim was never that statistics beat scouts. It was that a skill can be on sale.
sports.stats.moneyball.the-part-that-was.author: author-sports-niche-1

reviewed.notes: Payrolls corrected to sourced figures (A's about $44m, Yankees over $125m) and Lewis's book added as a source.

sports.stats.moneyball.the-part-that-was.body:
Oakland won 103 games in 2002 and reeled off 20 straight between 13 August and 4 September, on a player payroll of about \$44 million. The Yankees passed \$125 million that season. Michael Lewis turned it into *Moneyball* in 2003, and the world filed it under "nerds beat scouts".

That is not the claim. Oakland's edge was a *price* claim: the labour market for baseball players was paying a lot for batting average and stolen bases and almost nothing for on-base percentage, even though getting on base is what stops innings from ending. Billy Beane was not buying good players. He was buying an underpriced input.

And the tell that it was a price story, not a wisdom story, is what happened next. Hakes and Sauer ran the regressions in the *Journal of Economic Perspectives* in 2006: on-base percentage really was underpaid before the book, and within about two seasons after it, the discount was gone. The market read the book and repriced.

Which is the uncomfortable half. Every Moneyball edge destroys itself by being explained.

recall.question: What is the best evidence that Oakland's advantage was a market mispricing rather than superior judgement?

options.text: They won 103 games in 2002
options.why: a good season is consistent with skill, luck or mispricing; it does not distinguish them.

options.text: The pay premium for on-base percentage jumped within two years of the book's publication
options.why: a mispricing is something that can be arbitraged away once it is public, and it was.

options.text: Other clubs hired statisticians
options.why: adoption shows the idea spread, but not that the original edge was about price.

sports.stats.rankings.remember-eigenvect.title: Remember eigenvectors? Sports tables are full of them.
sports.stats.rankings.remember-eigenvect.hook: Beating a great team should count more than beating a bad one. Say that carefully and you have written down an eigenvalue problem.
sports.stats.rankings.remember-eigenvect.author: author-sports-niche-1

reviewed.notes: Keener 1993 confirmed via Crossref (SIAM Review 35(1):80-93). Removed the unsupported claim that his method ran inside the BCS formula.

sports.stats.rankings.remember-eigenvect.body:
An eigenvector is the direction a matrix leaves alone, up to scale. Here is where that turns into a league table.

Counting wins is a terrible ranking, and everyone knows why: it treats beating the champion and beating the bottom club as the same event. So try the obvious fix. *A team's rating should be proportional to the total rating of the teams it has beaten.* Say it out loud and notice what you have done — you have defined the rating vector in terms of itself.

Write $A$ for the matrix of results and $r$ for the vector of ratings. The sentence above says $Ar = \lambda r$. The ranking you wanted is an eigenvector, and the only sensible one is the dominant one.

James Keener wrote this up for *SIAM Review* in 1993, while American college football argued about whose computer ranking to trust. Callaghan, Mucha and Porter's random walker (2007) is the same fixed point in Markov disguise; so, on a matrix of links instead of results, is PageRank. Strength of schedule is not a bolt-on adjustment; it is what the eigenvector is *for*.

Existence and uniqueness are not free, though.
sports.stats.rankings.remember-eigenvect.rigor:
Let $a_{ij}\ge 0$ score team $i$'s results against $j$ (Keener uses a smooth, bounded function of the score line rather than raw margin, so a 50-point win cannot be farmed). Define ratings by

$$r_i=\frac{1}{\lambda}\sum_j a_{ij}r_j,\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad Ar=\lambda r .$$

**Perron–Frobenius.** If $A\ge 0$ is irreducible, it has a positive eigenvalue $\lambda_{\max}$ equal to its spectral radius, with a one-dimensional eigenspace spanned by a strictly positive vector, and no other eigenvector is nonnegative.

Unpack the hypotheses, because they are the sport. *Nonnegative* is free. *Irreducible* means the directed graph "i has a result against j" is strongly connected — every team reachable from every other through chains of fixtures. A league schedule gives you that; two conferences that never meet do not, and then the ranking between them is genuinely undefined, no matter what number a computer prints.

Positivity of the eigenvector is what makes the output a *ranking*: all ratings share a sign, so ratios are meaningful. And the power method converges to it, which is why these tables were computable in 1993 on the hardware of 1993.

recall.question: Two college conferences play a full schedule internally but never play each other. What breaks in the eigenvector ranking?

options.text: Nothing
options.why: the matrix is still nonnegative, and nonnegativity alone is enough for Perron–Frobenius.

options.text: Irreducibility fails, so the dominant eigenvector is no longer unique and the cross-conference comparison is arbitrary
options.why: the graph of results is not strongly connected.

options.text: The eigenvalues become complex
options.why: a nonnegative matrix always has a real spectral radius; the problem is uniqueness, not realness.

options.text: The power method diverges
options.why: it still converges within each block; the blocks just cannot be compared.
